segments.text: [MUSIC PLAYING]
DAN FIELD: Hi, everybody.
My name is Dan Field.
I'm a software engineer with the Flutter team.
VICTOR TSARAN: Hi, my name is Victor Tsaran.
I'm a technical program manager at Google
working on accessibility in Material Design.
You hear us talk a lot about accessibility,
but actually, what does it mean?
Well, there's many, many definitions.
I would send you to Wikipedia, but I'll spare you some time.
What we mean here today is accessibility is
when user interfaces are usable by anyone, including
people with disabilities.
According to World Health Organization,
there are about over 1 billion people
with disabilities in the world.
Some of the examples include, for example,
people who are completely blind or have some vision,
for example, like myself.
And I still can do things with a computer.
I can use my mobile phone.
In fact, I do my job at Google thanks to technology.
Also people who are hard of hearing,
they cannot hear anything or they can hear some.
Also people who have physical disabilities,
they can't use their hands to type on the keyboard.
Or actually anyone.
Some of you may have gotten into some temporary-- what
we call temporary disabilities where you may have injured
your arm while doing skateboarding
or whatever else you guys like doing.
So these things do happen to all of us.
And technology is here to save us in some ways.
And we've been using technology since ancient times
to improve the lives.
For example, we invented the wheel, fire, you know,
typewriter, smartphone, and so on and so forth.
And accessibility is a way to make technology work
for everyone, including people with disabilities.
Specifically for Flutter, why we're really
so passionate about accessibility in Flutter
is because Flutter is this cross-platform solution that
reaches millions of users out there.
And through implementing accessibility
in a consistent and friendly way for different platforms,
we can make it easier on developers, as well
as for users to ensure that they have a consistent experience
no matter which platform they're on.
DAN FIELD: Thanks, Victor.
So how does accessibility work in Flutter?
There's a few different areas to think about when
you think about accessibility.
It could be things like text contrast or screen readers,
tap targets, the size of things that you
want users to be able to interact with on your screen.
At a basic level, a really easy way to break this down
is when we think of Flutter, I think
we tend to think of the widgets that we create for our app.
And up on the screen here, I have a screenshot
of the Hello World Flutter app that you're probably
familiar with if you've ever done a Flutter Create
application starting out.
Each of these widgets corresponds to some number
of semantic tree nodes.
So we have the widgets tree and we also have a semantics tree.
Up on the screen here, you can see
that we have our header with the Flutter Demo Home Page,
which will have a semantics node that will say Flutter Demo Home
Page and is annotated as a header.
In the middle of the screen, "you have pushed the button
this many times."
There's another node with 1 as the counter
for the number of times you've pushed the button.
And then down towards the bottom,
there's that floating action button,
which has an Increment tooltip or label on it.
And that will also get annotated as being a button.
The widget tree does not necessarily
correspond one-to-one with the semantics tree in Flutter.
So some number of widget nodes may
get merged into a single semantic node
or you might have the opposite, where
what you think of as a single widget,
you actually want read out as more than one
semantic node for some reason.
For example, that header node up at the top, that's
an app bar with a text child.
That all gets one semantic node.
The two pieces of text in the middle,
they're each getting their own semantic node.
That button down at the bottom is actually multiple widgets
composed together for the shape of the button,
that it's a button, the label, the icon on the button,
and so forth, but that all gets one semantics node in the end.
Accessibility can be free.
So the Flutter framework has been
designed to be accessible out of the box.
There are all of the stock widgets that you'd want to use.
As long as you're filling in the relevant properties,
they will be accessible.
So for example on the screen now,
I have two different styles of button--
that floating action button and in the screenshot here,
I have the tooltip activated.
You can see it says, Increment.
The framework is smart enough to know
that because you put the tooltip widget in here,
it will create a button semantic node that says tooltip
as the label.
Similarly for our raised material button on the bottom,
it says Open on it.
That Open is a text child.
But again, the framework's smart enough to know,
this is a button that should say Open on it.
Sometimes it's not going to come by default, if, for example,
you have a really custom button that's just using a raw gesture
detector as opposed to using one of the out-of-the-box button
widgets.
Or like some of our speakers spoke about earlier,
if you're painting things directly
on a canvas with a custom painter,
or something like a single child render
object widget in those cases, you're
going to need to do a bit more work to tell Flutter how
to create the semantics tree.
So bespoke experiences need bespoke semantics.
Just like, as a designer, you're going
to spend a significant amount of time thinking
about how well my user interacts visually with this app, what's
it going to look like, how is this animation
or transition going to work, what kind of motion am I using,
we also want to think about how is a user going
to interact with my app if they're
using assistive technology like a screen reader.
As an example of this, we took a look at the Shrine app
from the new Flutter gallery.
And actually this is somewhat similar to the Shrine app
in the current Flutter gallery.
So if you're familiar with that, it's more or less the same.
I have an animation up here of some interactions
with the shrine app there is a dropdown
menu from the top left.
That lets you filter different products.
There's a list of products that you can scroll
in the middle of the screen.
And then down there at the bottom
there's a Cart button which, if you have products in it,
you can tap it, see what you've added,
remove products, or clear your whole cart.
At a very sort of boiled down, simplified level,
we have a stack widget that has a fancy app
bar with a dropdown, a special list view that gives us
these scattered products, and a shopping cart which
can be expanded or collapsed.
Obviously the real app's a bit more complicated than this.
But for our purposes here, this is good enough.
Now, we're going to want to look at how
a user with a screen reader would interact with this.
And Victor, you can tell us a bit more about TalkBack
and how that work.
VICTOR TSARAN: Just for today's session's purposes,
we decided to use TalkBack, which is a built-in screen
view on Android.
And you won't see me in that video,
but you will see me using the app.
And so a quick primer on how screen reader works-- there's
really few things you need to know.
When the user touches the screen, somebody
who's completely blind, they will hear spoken feedback--
or they should hear if everything works right.
When you swipe right, you go to the next element,
you swipe left to go to the previous element,
and if you want to activate the element
of your choice or that interests you, you'd have to double-tap.
So why don't we watch a video of me
trying to use the Shrine app before any accessibility markup
was applied.
DAN FIELD: Great.

VICTOR TSARAN: That was painful, right?
[AUDIENCE CHUCKLING]
Well, there are a few things that just happened-- well,
actually, that didn't happen.
Some of them did happen and some didn't.
Well, the first thing you may have noticed
is that when I was swiping between elements,
I was actually going through some elements
that I wasn't supposed to hear or see,
because they were actually invisible on the screen,
and yet my screen reader was able to get to them.
So that was not nice.
The bigger issue was-- well, the second big issue
was that when I was going through the buttons,
I wasn't exactly sure if I hit that button, if I double-tap
on it, what was supposed to happen.
Which, visually, you probably knew
clicking the button would actually add
the item to the shopping cart.
But that would be only part of the problem.
The biggest, biggest, biggest issue
was that I wasn't even able to get to the shopping cart.
What's the purpose of this app, right?
Really to get you buy things.
And so then-- and the team--
take it from here.
DAN FIELD: Sure.
So what can we do about this?
Some of these problems are widgets
that had properties that could have been set,
and didn't have them.
So for example, we had an image in there at one point--
it went pretty quick--
that really isn't relevant to someone using a screen reader.
Images have a property called Exclude from Semantics.
If they're purely there for just sort of visual flair,
and they have no real semantic meaning,
we should just go ahead exclude them.
We can use semantics widgets to specially annotate widgets
that are otherwise not quite getting the right thing.
This can be used to control things like sort order,
whether or not something's actually
a button, if it is a button, what do we want TalkBack
to say it does when you tap it?
Instead of just "double-tap to activate,"
could we make it say something better?
Using merge semantics to pull certain nodes together that
might have been separated-- we didn't see an example of that
in the video--
or using exclude semantics.
All right, so a couple examples of what
we went through and did to improve the screen reader
experience.
For that rolldown menu of the filtering products--
and that's what you saw, the screen reader
was jumping to invisible elements--
there's actually two ways we could have approached it.
So I'll first talk about what we actually end up doing here.
But I'll mention another.
We use an ExcludeSemantics.
A stack widget paints multiple widgets on top of each other.
And based on the state, you can control
where those widgets are positioned
and whether they're going to animate in, or out, and so
forth.
We want to actually just exclude the semantics based on
whether or not a certain property is set to true.
So it's very easy here to just add ExcludeSemantics widgets
to our tree.
And this way, when the menu is not visible,
it will not be part of the semantic tree
and it will not show up in the screen reader.
Another strategy we could've taken here--
and actually might have been a better one for this particular
example--
is to just exclude those widgets entirely
from the tree in this case.
So only have that background widget
there if we want to make the background part visible.
But you can imagine cases where there
is caching work being done there that you'd
benefit from building it even before it's
visible, and so forth.
And in that case, we still want to exclude the semantics
so that the screen reader doesn't
present a confusing or out-of-order experience.
Another thing that we did is we realized that the cart--
there were two problems with cart.
One, it wasn't reachable at all.
It turned out that another member of the team,
while working on the semantics for that Back floating action
button that you'll see again, they actually
put the semantics node around something that
ended up covering the cart.
When they tested it for the back node, it looked like it was OK.
But they had never realized it ended up covering the cart.
So that was one problem.
Another problem was, even after we
got the cart uncovered so that it looked
like it was visible in the semantics tree,
it was down as the last thing.
And you saw Victor had to scroll all the way
through a large number of products, which
could be sort of a deterrent to someone
actually using the app going to check out.
So for this we used a sort order key.
In our stack here, we have two semantics nodes
with a sortKey, one with the ordinal sortKey as 1,
and then the second one--
that paints later and comes semantically later--
with a sort ordinal key of 0.
This means when Flutter builds the semantics tree
for this application, the shopping cart
is going to come first.
And you'll know easily how to get back and forth
to the shopping cart.
There are gestures in TalkBack that you very quickly
navigate to the first or last item on the screen.
So with that, let's look at how our application changed
after applying some of these fixes.

VICTOR TSARAN: So if you have noticed, for this changes,
first of all, I didn't see those invisible elements,
which was nice.
I didn't care about them anyway in the first place.
The second thing, I actually could hear really nice hints
coming from TalkBack telling me to double-tap
to add to shopping cart, which is much friendlier
than just saying to double-tap to activate.
That was really cool.
But the coolest thing here, I was finally
able to find the shopping cart.
And you noticed, as I was adding items to the shopping cart,
the widget would actually reflect
the number of items in the shopping cart
at that particular moment.
And when I opened the shopping cart and removed items
one by one, that widget was also reflecting the number of items
left in the shopping cart.
So that was a much, much, much smoother and nicer experience.
And if you wonder, the same experience
would be available to anyone who is using VoiceOver screen
reader on iOS.
Because remember, Flutter is cross-platform.
And so in that sense, we've achieved, basically,
accessibility across platform.
DAN FIELD: Great.
So how can we test with TalkBack?
Maybe you're thinking, this is great,
but I've never done this before.
A really great way to start is just,
when you're going through your development process
on a physical device, enable accessibility services.
Turn on VoiceOver on iOS, or turn on TalkBack on Android,
and just see, what is this like?
Is this usable for me, as someone that's never even tried
to use it before?
It does have to be a physical device, because the emulators
and simulators don't quite provide the same accessibility
experience.
That's not so much a Flutter limitation
as just the state of the world right now.
Check your app with different text scaling options.
In Accessibility Services on most platforms,
users will have options to scale text up by as many
as, say, three times.
This is great for visual users that
have, say, vision impairment or vision difficulties.
What does your app look like when that happens?
Are you seeing weird overflows that you weren't expecting?
Is text flying off the screen now
because it's bigger than you were anticipating before?
And maybe have a hard-coded value
somewhere that you have to update,
or something that wasn't quite as responsive as it should be.
And then write widget unit tests--
semantics are enabled by default when Flutter runs unit tests.
This is not necessarily the case when Flutter runs on a device.
We only enable the semantics tree
if you have Accessibility Services turned on
like TalkBack or VoiceOver.
Or on Android, actually, there are some other applications
that may request the user turn it
on for some other accessibility reason other than screen
reading.
If you never test with Accessibility Services turned
on, at least your widget test will.
And it may catch issues that you otherwise would have missed.
In particular, I'm going to highlight a few things here
that the team has come up with to sort of help
you determine if your widget is accessible or not.
One of them is finding a widget by semantic label.
So if you've ever written a Flutter unit test,
you probably have thought of finding something
by the text label.
That's like Find.text.1 finds one widget, right?
That would return true for the screen up here.
Find.bySemanticsLabel increment will also
return true, because that button down there
has a tooltip of increment.
And this can be a great way to make sure
that, for a given widget or on a given screen,
a screen reader would be able to find the label that you're
expecting it to find.
Another good one is textContrastGuidelines.
So on the screen, highlighted here,
are places where there's text, including
the button, because that's actually a font icon.
This test will automatically rasterize the widget there,
and check, based on the WCAG accessibility contrast
guidelines, is your widget readable?
Is there sufficient contrast so that you meet those guidelines?
And this will basically just test the whole screen
that is currently in the test.
And then, finally, we have some around tap target sizes, one
for Android and iOS, which have slightly different guidelines
on how big a tap target should be.
So are my buttons big enough so that a user can tap them?
This is going to be particularly important for someone
with, say, motor impairment.
Or even if they don't have motor impairment,
they have larger fingers, or they
have trouble pinpointing a specific location on the screen
with their finger.
I have that problem a lot.
There's also-- are tap targets labeled?
When a screen reader comes to something that's tappable,
it's going to say, this is a button.
You want it to say, this is a button that does
"fill in the blank," or, this is the button for--
If you have a label on there, you're
going to get a much better experience.
If you don't, this test will catch.
You have a button in this widget that-- or a tap target
somewhere in this widget.
Maybe use a custom gesture detector or something
like that.
And it's not properly labeled.
So this is a great opportunity to make sure
that you follow these guidelines and that you'll have a better
experience for your users.
Finally, where can you go to get help?
So Flutter has documentation on accessibility available
on our website.
It provides a little bit more overview of some of the widgets
I pointed out, like Semantics, and MergeSemantics,
and so forth, a little bit more information on
how to activate screen readers on your chosen platform,
and how to test with them.
There's also the Material Design Accessibility site,
which is, if you're using Material
Design, a great resource for how to make
sure your components are accessible.
And then, finally, each other-- we
have a great community with Flutter.
And we have some great community resources listed
at flutter.dev/community, where we can turn to each other
and look for help and advice, making sure we're designing not
just for the visual, but also designing for all of our users,
and make sure we're reachable for everyone.
VICTOR TSARAN: Yeah, and with that, thank you so much.
DAN FIELD: Thank you very much.
